entry: Political and legal principle holding that law is clear, consistent and open, that people have access to justice, and that government institutions are subject to the law. The principle is often summarized as "no one is above the law" or "all are equal before the law." Legal scholars stress that laws must apply equally to everyone; "formalists" add that they must be stable, accessible and clear, while "substantivists" include rights such as [[Human rights|human rights]] and compliance with [[International law|international law]]. The phrase dates to 16th-century Britain and was popularized in the 19th century by British jurist A. V. Dicey. The principle, if not the phrase, was recognized by ancient thinkers such as [[Aristotle]]. It is the opposite of the "rule of man," in which one person or group rules arbitrarily.

Instrument for making length measurements by reading a length from a series of markings along an edge; also called a rule, scale, line gauge or [[Metre|metre]] stick. The instrument is usually rigid, and its edge can serve as a straightedge for drawing straight lines. Rulers are important tools in geometry, geography and mathematics. The oldest preserved measuring rod is a copper-alloy bar dating from c. 2650 BC, found at the [[Sumer|Sumerian]] city of Nippur in present-day Iraq. Rulers of [[Ivory|ivory]] were in use in the Indus Valley Civilization before 1500 BC. Many distance units were based on the human body, such as the [[Cubit|cubit]], hand and foot. Historically, rulers were mainly made of [[Wood|wood]], but [[Plastic|plastics]] are also used, and metal rulers serve durable workshop needs. Anton Ullrich invented the folding ruler in 1851.

Liquor made by fermenting and then distilling sugarcane [[Molasses|molasses]] or sugarcane juice, often aged in barrels. Rum originated in the [[Caribbean]] in the 17th century, where it was likely first created by enslaved people on sugar plantations, and it is now produced in nearly every major sugar-producing region of the world. Light rums are commonly used in cocktails, while aged or dark rums are often drunk straight, iced or used in cooking. Historically, rum played a role in the triangular trade, the slave trade and colonial economies of the West Indies and British colonies. It has deep cultural associations with the [[Royal Navy]] and maritime history, and it has been used to fund organized crime and military insurgencies such as the [[American Revolution]].

Hoofed herbivorous grazing or browsing mammal of the suborder Ruminantia. Ruminants digest plant fibers such as [[Cellulose|cellulose]] by fermenting them in a specialized stomach, principally through microbial action, a process called foregut fermentation. The fermented ingesta, known as cud, is regurgitated and chewed again in a process called rumination. The roughly 200 species include [[Cattle|cattle]], goats, sheep, giraffes, deer, gazelles and antelopes. Ruminants are the most diverse group of living [[Ungulate|ungulates]]. The suborder includes six families: Tragulidae, Giraffidae, Antilocapridae, Cervidae, Moschidae and Bovidae. The first fossil ruminants appeared in the Early Eocene. The word comes from Latin rūminārī, "to ruminate," from rūmen, the first stomach.

1977 studio album by the British and American rock band [[Fleetwood Mac]]. Largely recorded in California in 1976, amid breakups among band members and heavy drug use, its lyrics concern personal and often troubled relationships. *Rumours* was the band's first UK number-one album, topped the U.S. Billboard 200, and won Album of the Year at the 1978 Grammy Awards. As of February 2023 it had sold over 40 million copies worldwide. It was selected for the National Recording Registry in 2017 by the [[Library of Congress]].

German [[Fairy tale|fairy tale]] collected by the [[Brothers Grimm]] and first published in the 1812 edition of *Children's and Household Tales*. A miller boasts that his daughter can spin straw into [[Gold|gold]]. An imp spins it for her in exchange for her necklace, her ring and finally her firstborn child. When the queen bears that child, the imp returns to claim it, but she has three days to guess his name. She discovers it, and in the 1812 edition the imp "ran away angrily, and never came back." Later versions give a more violent ending.

American [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] group formed in Hollis, [[Queens]], [[New York City]], in 1983. The members were Joseph Simmons, Darryl McDaniels and Jason Mizell. Regarded as one of the most influential acts in hip-hop history, the group was among the first to popularize the MC and DJ relationship and helped usher in golden age hip-hop. Its 1984 album *Run-D.M.C.* made it the first hip-hop group to achieve a gold record, and *Raising Hell* (1986) became the first multi-platinum hip-hop record. Its cover of "Walk This Way" with [[Aerosmith]] peaked at number four on the Billboard Hot 100, higher than Aerosmith's original version. The group was the first hip-hop act to have its videos broadcast on [[MTV]] and to perform at [[Live Aid]], and it was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2009.

Letters of related alphabets, known as futharks or runic alphabets, native to the Germanic peoples. Runes primarily represented sounds, though some also stood for the concepts after which they are named. Runology is the academic study of runic alphabets and inscriptions. The earliest secure runic inscriptions date from AD 150 at the latest. Runes were generally replaced by the [[Latin alphabet|Latin alphabet]] as the cultures that used them were Christianized, by about AD 700 in central Europe and 1100 in northern Europe, though they persisted for specialized purposes. The three best-known alphabets are the Elder Futhark (c. AD 150–800), the Anglo-Saxon Futhorc (400–1100) and the Younger Futhark (800–1100). The script ultimately stems from the [[Phoenician alphabet|Phoenician alphabet]].

Family of explicit and implicit iterative methods in [[Numerical analysis|numerical analysis]] for approximating solutions of [[Differential equation|differential equations]]. Developed around 1900 by the German mathematicians Carl Runge and Wilhelm Kutta. The best-known member, RK4, uses a weighted average of four slope estimates per step; its local truncation error is on the order of O(h⁵), and its total accumulated error is on the order of O(h⁴). If f is independent of y, RK4 is Simpson's rule.

Method of terrestrial locomotion by which humans and other animals move quickly on foot. Running has an aerial phase in which both or all feet are above the ground at some stage, in contrast to [[Walking|walking]], in which at least one foot is always in contact with the ground. The term covers speeds from jogging to sprinting. Running in humans is associated with improved health and [[Life expectancy|life expectancy]]. Competitive running grew out of religious festivals in areas including Greece, Egypt and Asia, and the first recorded Olympic Games took place in 776 BCE. Early humans most likely became endurance runners through persistence [[Hunting|hunting]], following and chasing prey until it was too exhausted to flee. Running has been described as the world's most accessible sport.

Australian-born American business magnate and media executive. Through News Corp he owns hundreds of publishing outlets, including *The Sun* and *The Times* in the United Kingdom, *The Wall Street Journal* and the *New York Post* in the United States, and [[Fox News]] through Fox Corporation. Born and raised in [[Melbourne]], he took over the running of *The News*, a small [[Adelaide]] newspaper, after his father died in 1952. He expanded into the United Kingdom in 1969, moved to New York City in 1974, and became a naturalized American citizen in 1985. His papers and channels have been accused of right-wing bias, and in 2011 his companies faced allegations of phone hacking, including at the *News of the World*. In 2023 he announced that he would step down as chairman of Fox Corp. and News Corp.

Geographic area located outside towns and cities, typically with low population density and small settlements. Agricultural and forested land is typically described as rural, and definitions vary by country and purpose. Rural economies depend on land-based industries such as [[Agriculture|agriculture]], [[Forestry|forestry]] and resource extraction, and they are vulnerable to boom-and-bust cycles and extreme weather such as [[Drought|droughts]]. Economic forces encouraging [[Urbanization|urbanization]] have led to rural flight, in which younger people move to cities for education and jobs, leaving older and less wealthy populations behind. According to the Food and Agricultural Organization, three quarters of the global impoverished live in rural areas. Some communities have encouraged development through access to electricity or internet.

Dynasty that ruled [[Kievan Rus']] and its successor principalities. According to tradition, the Varangian prince Rurik founded it by establishing himself at Novgorod in 862, though modern scholars regard him as a legendary figure. After Kievan Rus' disintegrated, the house split into independent principalities. The Daniilovichi of [[Moscow]] unified the northern and northeastern territories, and by the 15th century Ivan III had thrown off the control of the [[Golden Horde]]. The Rurik line ruled until 1598, when it was succeeded by the [[House of Romanov]]. The dynasty held power for 21 generations in male-line succession, a period of more than 700 years. Numerous princely families have claimed descent from Rurik.

Canadian rock band formed in [[Toronto]] in 1968. Its classic power trio of guitarist Alex Lifeson, bassist and vocalist Geddy Lee and drummer Neil Peart was stable from 1974 until Peart retired in 2015. Known for complex compositions and lyrics drawing on science fiction, fantasy and philosophy, the band moved from blues-inspired hard rock to progressive rock, then to heavy use of [[Synthesizer|synthesizers]] in the 1980s, before returning to guitar-driven rock. Rush was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2013, and music critics consider it one of the greatest rock bands of all time.

New Zealand–born actor and film director. Crowe moved to Australia at age four and was living there permanently by age 21. He won the AACTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role for his breakthrough role in *Romper Stomper* (1992) and gained international recognition with *L.A. Confidential* (1997) and *The Insider* (1999). He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Gladiator* (2000) and was nominated for playing [[John Forbes Nash Jr.]] in *A Beautiful Mind* (2001). His directorial debut was *The Water Diviner* (2014). He has been co-owner of the South Sydney Rabbitohs since 2006.

Set-theoretic paradox published by the British philosopher and mathematician [[Bertrand Russell]] in 1901. It shows that every set theory with an unrestricted comprehension principle leads to contradictions. Let R be the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. If R is not a member of itself, then by definition it is a member of itself; if it is, then by definition it is not. Russell also showed that a version of the paradox could be derived in the axiomatic system of the German philosopher and mathematician [[Gottlob Frege]], undermining Frege's attempt to reduce mathematics to logic. Two influential ways of avoiding it were proposed in 1908: Russell's own type theory and Zermelo set theory, which restricted the unlimited comprehension principle. Ernst Zermelo had discovered the paradox independently by 1902, but he did not publish it.

Military of the Russian Federation, organized into the Ground Forces, Navy and Aerospace Forces. Its three independent combat arms are the Strategic Rocket Forces, Airborne Forces and Unmanned Systems Forces. It is the world's fifth-largest military force, with about one million active-duty personnel and close to two million reservists, and it maintains the world's largest stockpile of nuclear weapons. Despite efforts to professionalize since the early 2000s, it remains heavily reliant on conscripts. The [[Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)|Russo-Ukrainian war]] has exposed weaknesses such as [[Corruption|corruption]], rigid command and control, inadequate training and poor morale.

Pedigreed cat breed with a solid blue coat. It has a dense, plush double coat of pale blue-grey fur with a distinct silver sheen, and bright emerald green to yellow-green eyes. It holds championship status with all major international cat registries. It may have originated in the port of Arkhangelsk in [[Russia]], and sailors are believed to have taken the cats to Britain in the 1860s. After [[World War II]], a shortage of the breed led to crossbreeding with Siamese cats, and US breeders then combined Scandinavian and British bloodlines to create the modern breed.

Multi-party civil war in the former Russian Empire, lasting from 1917 to 1922. It was sparked by the overthrow of the Provisional Government in the [[October Revolution]]. The two largest combatants were the [[Red Army]], fighting for a [[Bolsheviks|Bolshevik]]-led socialist state headed by [[Vladimir Lenin]], and the White movement, led mainly by right-leaning officers of the former imperial army. Ukrainian anarchists, Left Socialist-Revolutionaries and non-ideological green armies also opposed the Bolsheviks, and 13 foreign states intervened against the Red Army. The Bolsheviks initially consolidated control over most of the former empire, and the war ended with the capture of [[Vladivostok]] in October 1922. It resulted in the formation of the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic and later the [[Soviet Union]]. An estimated 7 to 12 million casualties, mostly civilians, resulted.

Final phase of the Russian monarchy, spanning most of northern Eurasia from 1721 until the proclamation of the Russian Republic in 1917. At its height in the late 19th century it covered approximately 22,800,000 km² (8,800,000 sq mi), making it the third-largest empire in history after the British and Mongol empires. [[Peter the Great]] (r. 1682–1725) transformed the tsardom into an empire and moved the capital from [[Moscow]] to [[Saint Petersburg]]. [[Catherine the Great]] (r. 1762–1796) presided over further expansion. Defeat in the [[Crimean War]] (1853–1856) prompted domestic reform, and Alexander II (r. 1855–1881) initiated major reforms, including the 1861 emancipation of approximately 23 million serfs. Following the 1905 Revolution, Nicholas II (r. 1894–1917) authorized the State Duma, though ultimate authority remained with him. Military setbacks and food shortages in World War I led to the February Revolution of 1917, which led to his abdication.

Autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church, also officially known as the Moscow Patriarchate. It is the largest Eastern Orthodox church by number of adherents, and its primate is the Patriarch of Moscow and all Rus'. Christianization of Kievan Rus' began in 988 with the baptism of [[Vladimir the Great]] by clergy of the [[Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople|Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople]]. The church declared autocephaly in 1448 and became a patriarchate in 1589. In the mid-17th century liturgical reforms led to a schism, and opponents formed the [[Old Believers]]. [[Peter the Great]] abolished the patriarchate in 1721, and it was restored in 1917. Under Soviet state atheism the church was heavily persecuted, but it experienced a major revival beginning in the late 1980s. In 2018 it severed communion with the Ecumenical Patriarchate after the latter recognized the autocephaly of the Orthodox Church of [[Ukraine]].

Period of political and social upheaval in Russia beginning in 1917, which ended the monarchy and established a socialist government. It began with the February Revolution, after which [[Nicholas II]] abdicated and a provisional government took power. Soviet councils formed in Petrograd held domestic power alongside it, and the [[Bolsheviks]], led by [[Vladimir Lenin]], promised peace, land and bread. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution, an armed insurrection that overthrew the provisional government. They signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918, and the Cheka secret police carried out the Red Terror. A civil war followed, in which [[Leon Trotsky]] organized the [[Red Army]]. Historians consider the revolutionary period to have ended in 1922, when the civil war concluded with the defeat of the White Army.

First Russian Revolution, a wave of political and social unrest in the Russian Empire beginning in 1905. On January 22, 1905, troops fired on a peaceful procession of workers led by Georgy Gapon outside the tsar's Winter Palace in [[Saint Petersburg]], an event known as "Bloody Sunday." Strikes and peasant revolts spread across the empire, and sailors on the battleship *Potemkin* mutinied. A general strike in October led [[Nicholas II]] to issue the October Manifesto, promising a legislative assembly and expanded rights. The first State Duma was dissolved in July 1906, and Pyotr Stolypin restored autocratic rule. Many historians consider the revolution to have set the stage for 1917, and [[Vladimir Lenin|Lenin]] later called it the "dress rehearsal" for the [[October Revolution]].

Literature of Russia, its émigrés and Russian-language writers. Written literature traces its roots to the Early Middle Ages, when Old Church Slavonic was introduced as a literary language. From the early 1830s, Russian literature entered a "Golden Age" in poetry, prose and drama, led by [[Alexander Pushkin|Pushkin]], [[Fyodor Dostoevsky|Dostoevsky]], [[Leo Tolstoy|Tolstoy]] and [[Anton Chekhov|Chekhov]]. The Silver Age at the end of the 19th century produced poets such as [[Anna Akhmatova|Akhmatova]]. After the [[Russian Revolution]] of 1917, literature split into Soviet and émigré parts; the Soviet state imposed ideological censorship, and socialist realism became predominant in the 1930s. [[Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn|Solzhenitsyn]], a Nobel Prize-winning novelist, opposed Soviet ideology, while Varlam Shalamov wrote about the [[Gulag|gulag]] camps. Russia has five Nobel Prize in Literature laureates.

War in August 2008 waged by the Russian Federation and the Russian-backed separatist regions of [[South Ossetia]] and [[Abkhazia]] against [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]. Regarded as the first European war of the 21st century, it followed Georgian army units' entry into the South Ossetian conflict zone on 7 August. Russia accused Georgia of genocide and launched a full-scale invasion on 8 August. French president [[Nicolas Sarkozy]] negotiated a ceasefire on 12 August. The war displaced approximately 192,000 people across Georgia, and on 26 August Russia recognized Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.
